Nuts and seeds, especially walnuts and flaxseed

The common thread: whole, unprocessed foods eaten slowly and mindfully, without constant snacking, give your gut the best environment to produce GLP-1 naturally and keep appetite perfectly regulated.

doc_title: Lesson 6: GLP-1 and Appetite Regulation
heading: Key Insight
text: GLP-1 agonist medications carry up to 9.09 times higher risk of pancreatitis and cause up to 40% of total weight loss to come from lean muscle mass rather than fat.

doc_title: Lesson 6: GLP-1 and Appetite Regulation
heading: What You Just Learned
text:
- GLP-1 is released naturally in response to eating and regulates insulin secretion, stomach emptying speed, and satiety signals to the brain.
- Synthetic GLP-1 drugs carry severe risks — pancreatitis, gastroparesis, bowel obstruction — and cause catastrophic muscle mass loss.
- Protein, healthy fats, fermented foods, and dietary fiber all naturally stimulate your own GLP-1 production without any pharmaceutical risk.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Overview
text:
Movement in nature supports leptin and ghrelin balance

While GLP-1 manages the immediate feeling of fullness after a meal, your long-term energy balance and daily hunger cues are controlled by a constant dialogue between two other major hormones: Leptin and Ghrelin. If you constantly feel like you are battling your appetite, it is rarely a failure of willpower. It is almost always a miscommunication between these hormones.

Because the brain cannot sense the leptin, it assumes the body is starving — and responds by dramatically increasing appetite and slowing the metabolic rate to conserve every calorie.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Leptin: The Energy Gauge
text:
Leptin is the hormone of satiety, but unlike GLP-1 (which comes from your gut), Leptin is produced directly by your fat cells. Its primary job is to act as a fuel gauge for your brain. As you store energy in your fat cells, they release leptin into the bloodstream. This leptin travels to the hypothalamus in your brain, delivering a simple message: "We have plenty of stored energy. We don't need to eat right now, and it is safe to maintain a high metabolic rate."

In a healthy system, this works perfectly. If you overeat for a few days, your fat cells release more leptin, your appetite naturally drops, your desire to move increases, and your body weight auto-regulates.

However, if you are struggling with weight, this system is likely disrupted by a condition called Leptin Resistance. When insulin is chronically elevated (from frequent eating and high carbohydrate consumption), it actively blocks the leptin signal from reaching the brain. You may have plenty of stored energy in your fat cells, and those fat cells may be shouting at your brain to stop eating, but the high insulin acts like static on the radio. The brain never hears the message.

Because the brain cannot sense the leptin, it assumes the body is starving. It responds exactly how a starving body should: it drastically increases your appetite and slows down your metabolic rate to conserve energy. This is why people with insulin resistance are often intensely hungry despite having excess stored body fat. To fix leptin resistance and restore your body’s natural energy gauge, you must first lower insulin.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: It's the Same Thing That Happened With Insulin
text:
There's another layer to this, and once you see it the whole picture clicks.

In Lesson 2 you learned that insulin resistance isn't your cells breaking. It's your cells turning down the volume on a signal that never stops shouting.

Leptin does exactly the same thing.

The more fat you store, the more leptin you produce. And when leptin stays high month after month, year after year, the receptors in your brain stop responding fully to it.

Your fat cells are shouting we have plenty of energy here — and your brain has stopped listening, for the same protective reason it stopped listening to insulin. A cell that kept responding fully to a hormone flooding it all day, every day, for twenty years would be in far worse shape.

So it's one disease wearing two costumes. Too much signal, for too long, and the receiver turns down the volume. Insulin and leptin resistance travel together, worsen each other, and respond to the same things.

Which is also why the fix isn't a leptin supplement or a leptin drug. You can't shout louder at a system that stopped listening because of the shouting. You have to let it go quiet.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: So How Do You Get the Signal Working Again?
text:
Lowering insulin is the main lever and it's where most of this book lives. But leptin resistance has several inputs — and if your food is already sorted and nothing has changed, the answer is probably here.

Reduce inflammation. Inflammation in your brain's appetite center directly interferes with leptin's signal. This is why Lessons 10, 11, and 14 — ceramides, gut health, and processed food — are leptin chapters even though they never use the word.

Lower your triglycerides. There's research suggesting triglycerides can cross into the brain and directly impair both leptin and insulin signalling there. That's animal research, so hold it loosely — but it connects the triglyceride-to-HDL ratio from Lesson 3 straight to this chapter. One number, two systems.

Sleep. One bad night raises ghrelin and lowers leptin. Chronic short sleep keeps both pointed the wrong way, every single day. This is not a small lever.

Build and keep muscle. Muscle changes where energy goes and how much insulin is needed to put it there. Lesson 17.

Cut liquid fructose specifically. Sugary drinks appear to worsen leptin signalling, and fructose goes straight to the liver. Lesson 11.

And give it time. Leptin resistance took years to develop. It doesn't reverse in a week, and the early stages of improvement often feel like nothing is happening at all. That's not failure — that's the timeline.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Adiponectin: The One That Falls
text:
Your fat tissue isn't a storage unit. It's an endocrine organ — it manufactures hormones and sends messages — and leptin isn't the only one.

Adiponectin is the useful counterpart, and it behaves in the opposite direction.

Where leptin rises as you store more fat, adiponectin falls. And adiponectin is the helpful one: it improves insulin sensitivity, reduces inflammation, and encourages your cells to burn fat rather than store it.

So metabolic dysfunction has a signature at the hormonal level: leptin high and ineffective, adiponectin low. The signal you've stopped hearing is loud, and the signal that would actually help has gone quiet.

It also tells you something about which fat matters. Deep abdominal fat produces less adiponectin and more inflammatory signals than fat stored under the skin. Which is part of why your waist measurement tells you more about your metabolic health than your weight does — something worth remembering when the scale won't move.

The good news: adiponectin responds to the same things everything else in this book responds to. Losing visceral fat, reducing inflammation, and exercise.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Ghrelin: The Hunger Hormone
text:
Ghrelin is the hormone that makes your stomach growl. It is produced primarily in the stomach and acts as a direct signal to the brain that it is time to seek out food. Ghrelin levels naturally rise before your typical meal times and plummet immediately after you eat.

Interestingly, ghrelin is highly trainable and heavily influenced by your habits. If you consistently eat a snack at 2:00 PM every day, your body will begin surging ghrelin at 1:45 PM in anticipation. If you stop eating that snack, the ghrelin surge will be uncomfortable for a few days, but it will eventually adapt and disappear. Ghrelin is also deeply connected to your sleep cycle. Just one night of poor sleep significantly elevates ghrelin levels the following day while simultaneously lowering leptin. This means your brain is aggressively telling you to eat more while simultaneously ignoring the signals that tell you to stop. This is why cravings for high-sugar, high-energy foods are so intense when you are exhausted. Managing ghrelin is not about fighting hunger; it is about providing your body with nutrient-dense meals, adequate sleep, and stable eating windows so the hormone stops working against you.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Dessert Stomach Is Real
text:
One more quirk worth knowing, because it explains something everybody has experienced and nobody can explain.

Fullness is partly specific to the food you just ate.

Your brain gets tired of the flavor in front of it while staying fully interested in a different one. That's measurable — the brain's response to a food declines as you eat it, while its response to a different taste stays completely intact.

So after a large savory meal, you are genuinely full of savory and not remotely full of sweet. That's why the dessert menu still works, and it has nothing to do with how much room is left in your stomach.

This is useful to know, because it means a craving that appears right after a meal usually isn't hunger at all. It's a different channel opening up. Which is a very different problem, and it responds to different things — walking away from the table, brushing your teeth, or simply knowing what it is.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Why Your Body Fights Back — And Why It Isn't Your Fault
text:
There's a study I need to tell you about.

Researchers took 50 overweight adults through a ten-week weight loss program. Average loss: about 30 pounds. Then they measured their appetite hormones three times — at the start, at the end of the program, and a full year later.

What they found at ten weeks was expected. Leptin had dropped sharply. So had several other fullness hormones. And ghrelin — the hunger hormone — had gone up.

That makes sense. Less fat means less leptin. The body notices and starts pushing for food.

Here's the finding that matters.

A year later, those hormone changes had not gone back to normal. Leptin was still suppressed. Ghrelin was still elevated. And the participants still reported being hungrier than they were before they ever started.

The researchers' conclusion was blunt: one year after weight loss, the hormones that drive weight regain do not return to pre-weight-loss levels.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Read That Again and Think About Your Own History
text:
If you have lost weight and then, months later, found yourself fighting hunger in a way you never had to before — that was measurable. It was happening in your bloodstream. It was not motivation running out, or old habits creeping back, or a failure of commitment.

Your body quietly changed the terms. Less of the hormone that says we have enough. More of the hormone that says go find food. And it held those settings for at least a year.

Every time you were told you just needed to want it more, this was what was actually happening.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: One Detail That Points at Something Important
text:
In research comparing methods, diet-induced weight loss raised ghrelin substantially. People who lost the same weight through gastric bypass surgery didn't see the same rise — because the surgery removes part of the tissue that produces it.

Same weight lost. Different hormonal aftermath.

How you lose weight changes what your body does afterward. Which is the entire argument of this book.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
section: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: And Here's What It Changes
text:
If regain were about willpower, the answer would be to try harder.

Since it's about a hormonal environment that shifted underneath you, the answer is completely different: you have to keep sending the signals that tell your body it isn't in a famine.

Enough food. Enough protein. Enough sleep. Muscle you're actively maintaining. Not white-knuckling through hunger — because that's the approach that produced this in the first place.

This is not a reason to stop. It's the reason the method matters more than the number of pounds. A body that was fed properly while losing weight ends up in a different hormonal place than one that was starved into it.

You were never fighting your own weakness. You were fighting a headwind nobody told you about. Now you know it's there, and you know what actually works against it.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: Key Insight
text: Chronically elevated insulin physically blocks the leptin signal from reaching the brain — creating a state where the brain perceives starvation despite having abundant stored energy.

doc_title: Lesson 7: Other Key Metabolic Hormones: Leptin, Ghrelin, and Adiponectin
heading: What You Just Learned
text:
- Leptin resistance — caused by chronically high insulin — makes the brain perceive starvation even when the body holds abundant stored fat, driving relentless hunger.
- Ghrelin is a highly trainable hormone that responds directly to eating patterns, sleep quality, and meal timing consistency.
- Restoring leptin sensitivity requires lowering insulin through proper nutrition — not calorie restriction, which worsens the problem.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Overview
text:
Strength training accelerates metabolic flexibility

When we talk about shifting the body from a state of storing energy to a state of burning energy, we have to talk about ketones. Ketones are often misunderstood as just a fad diet trend, but they are actually a fundamental part of human biology and a sign of true metabolic flexibility.

When insulin levels are low—either through fasting, exercise, or restricting dietary carbohydrates—the body realizes it cannot rely on glucose for fuel. The liver then steps in and begins breaking down your stored body fat into fatty acids. However, the brain cannot use typical fatty acids for fuel. To solve this, the liver converts those fats into small, highly efficient energy molecules called ketones (specifically beta-hydroxybutyrate).

Worth being clear about why ketones exist.

It's your brain. Fatty acids can't get into your brain easily, so your liver converts them into ketones, which can.

Your other tissues don't need that step. Your muscles burn fat directly. So does your heart — in fact your heart runs mostly on fat all day long, and always has.

So ketones aren't how your body burns fat. They're the workaround for the one organ that can't. Everything else was already burning fat as it is.

When your body is fueled by its own stored fat via ketones, the blood sugar rollercoaster stops entirely — and energy levels remain stable throughout the entire day.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: The Ultimate Clean Fuel
text:
Ketones are often described as a "cleaner" burning fuel than glucose. When your mitochondria burn ketones for energy, they produce significantly fewer free radicals (oxidative stress) than they do when burning sugar. This reduces systemic inflammation at the cellular level.

Furthermore, ketones do more than just provide energy. They act as powerful signaling molecules. Research shows that elevated ketones can actually protect muscle tissue from breaking down, enhance brain function and focus, and directly suppress appetite. When your body is fueled by its own stored fat via ketones, the blood sugar rollercoaster stops. Energy levels remain stable throughout the day because you are tapping into a massive, nearly unlimited internal fuel tank rather than relying on the next meal.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Ketones Don't Just Feed Your Cells — They Instruct Them
text:
Here's something about ketones that goes beyond energy.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate acts as a signalling molecule that switches on your cells' own antioxidant defenses.

In a study published in Science, researchers found that BHB directly changes which genes your cells express — turning up the specific proteins that protect against oxidative damage. Mice given BHB in advance were dramatically protected against a poison that kills by generating exactly that kind of damage.

BHB also shuts down one of the main inflammatory switches in the body.

So ketones aren't only a fuel. They're an instruction to clean up. Which is the whole point of this book — the molecule isn't just energy, it's a message. And this one tells your cells to raise their defenses.

It's also why ketones do things that have nothing to do with weight. The research on brain protection and inflammation is about signalling, not calories.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: A Distinction That Will Save You Months
text:
Ketosis means your body is running on fat. It does not automatically mean it's running on your fat.

If you eat enough dietary fat, your body will happily burn that instead — staying in ketosis, ticking every box, and never reaching far into your own stores. You can be genuinely fat-adapted and genuinely not losing fat.

Every marker looks right. The strips are positive. Energy is good. Cravings are gone. And nothing changes.

And Here's the Mechanism, Because It Explains Everything

Your fat cells aren't a warehouse. They're a revolving door.

Fat is being released and repackaged constantly — right now, and while you sleep. And in fasting people, researchers have measured as much as 60% of the fatty acids released from fat cells being put straight back into storage rather than burned.

Released. Not burned. Repackaged. Your body even spends energy doing it — it costs six units of cellular energy currency to reattach three fatty acids.

So being in ketosis means the door is open. It doesn't tell you which direction the traffic is going.

And what determines the direction is simple: does your body actually need the energy? If you've eaten enough fat to cover your requirements, there's no reason to burn what you released. So it pays the cost and puts it back.

Which Means the Lever Is Usually Your Added Fats

If you're fully adapted, feeling well, and your body composition isn't moving, look at the added fats — the ones not attached to a protein. Butter in coffee, extra oil, fat bombs.

Those were genuinely useful during the transition. They quietly become the reason nothing is changing.

Lesson 9 has the full picture of how this cycle works.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: One Thing That Surprises People
text:
A meaningful minority of people — often the leanest and most metabolically healthy, which is the odd part — see their LDL cholesterol rise substantially on a low-carbohydrate diet. Sometimes a lot.

What to do if it happens:

Get an ApoB test. It counts the actual number of particles in your blood rather than the cholesterol inside them, and it's the number that tells you the most.

Look at the whole picture. Triglycerides down and HDL up alongside a higher LDL is a different situation from everything moving the wrong way.

And take it to your doctor rather than to the internet. There are loud voices on both sides of this and neither of them knows your history. This is genuinely unresolved, and anyone telling you it's simple — in either direction — is overselling.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: What "Opening the Gates" Actually Means
text:
I've used that phrase. Let me show you the real thing — because there is an actual gate.

Fat cannot burn itself. To be used for energy, a fat molecule has to be physically carried through a specific doorway into the part of your cell that burns fuel. It can't drift in.

That doorway is an enzyme called CPT-1.

And here's what matters. When you eat carbohydrate and insulin rises, your body produces a molecule whose entire job is building fat for storage. That molecule blocks the doorway.

So when insulin is up, the door is shut. Fat can be sitting right there inside the cell — plenty of it, right outside the furnace — completely unable to get in.

Not because you don't have fat to burn. Because the door is locked.

Lower insulin and the door opens. That's what carbohydrate restriction is actually doing, and it's why the amount of carbohydrate matters more than the calories attached to it.

And There's a Carrier

The door needs more than to be unlocked. Something has to carry the fat through it — a molecule called carnitine.

Your body builds carnitine from two amino acids, using vitamin C to assemble it.

Which is worth pausing on: your ability to burn fat depends on getting enough protein and enough vitamin C. The door can be wide open and still have nothing to carry fat through it.

This is also why medium-chain fats — the ones concentrated in coconut oil and MCT oil — behave differently. They don't need the door. They get in regardless of whether insulin has locked it, which is why they help during the transition.

Two Things That Take Two Different Amounts of Time

The door unlocking takes hours. It happens every night while you sleep.

Building more doors — and more furnaces to feed — takes weeks.

That's the difference between being allowed to burn fat and being good at it. And it's why week six feels nothing like week one.

And One More Thing

Muscle contraction unlocks the same door, from the other side.

Moving your body hits the exact same lock that insulin controls. Not indirectly — the same lock.

That's why a ten-minute walk after dinner does more than it looks like it should. Lesson 17.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Transitioning into Fat-Burning: The Keto Flu
text:
To actually reach a state of ketosis and produce these molecules, you must consistently keep your insulin levels low. For most people, this means restricting dietary carbohydrates to ideally under 40 grams per day. Some individuals, especially those with severe insulin resistance, may need to drop even lower (under 20 grams) to fully open the fat-burning gates.

However, if your body has relied on a constant stream of sugar for decades, it takes time to adjust. Your cellular machinery has to literally build new enzymes to remember how to burn fat for fuel. During this adaptation phase—which can last anywhere from a few days to a couple of weeks—you might experience fatigue, headaches, brain fog, or irritability. This is often referred to as the "keto flu."

The keto flu is not an actual sickness; rather, it is a temporary energy crisis combined with a sudden electrolyte and nutrient shift. As your insulin plummets, your kidneys naturally stop hoarding water and rapidly flush out excess sodium. At the same time, your mitochondria are working overtime to transition their fuel source.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Combating the Keto Flu
text:
The best way to combat the keto flu is twofold:

Replenish Electrolytes

You must purposefully replenish what is being flushed out. Do not fear salt. Liberally salt your food and drink plenty of water (even adding a pinch of high-quality sea salt to your glass) to prevent dehydration and muscle cramps.

Increase B Vitamins

B vitamins, particularly Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) and Vitamin B5 (Pantothenic Acid), are absolutely critical co-enzymes required by your mitochondria to process fat into usable energy. When you suddenly shift from burning carbs to burning fat, your cellular demand for B vitamins skyrockets. If you don't have enough, your energy production stalls, causing deep fatigue. Incorporating high-quality sources of B vitamins—like nutritional yeast, liver, or a high-quality B-complex supplement—can help your cells rapidly build their new fat-burning engines and eliminate the fatigue.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Testing, and Why Your Strips Stop Working
text:
Urine strips are cheap and useful for about the first two weeks. After that they become misleading.

Here's why, and it catches people out constantly: as you adapt, your body stops wasting ketones in your urine. It's getting better at using them. So the strips fade exactly when you're doing well — and a lot of people quit at that point thinking they fell out of ketosis.

A blood meter is the accurate option if you like data.

Or measure nothing. Once you're adapted, how you feel is a better guide than a number: stable energy, cravings gone, comfortable going five or six hours without food. If you have those, you have what you came for.

And Ketone Supplements?

You can buy ketones in a bottle. They do raise your blood ketone level.

What they don't do is make you burn your own fat. If anything they do the opposite in the moment — when ketones arrive from outside, your liver makes fewer of its own, because the signal to produce them has been satisfied. You're in ketosis without being in fat-burning.

They may help during the transition. They are not a shortcut, and a positive reading from a supplement tells you nothing about fat loss.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Why Keto Can Fail the Chronically Ill
text:
While ketosis is a powerful tool for reversing insulin resistance, it is not for everyone. If your body is in a state of cellular energy failure—due to severe chronic illness (like Epstein-Barr Virus), extreme stress, or years of chronic dieting—a strict low-carb diet can act as a dangerous physiological stressor that keeps the body trapped in survival mode.

When the body is deeply stressed, it cannot efficiently "switch" to producing ketones. Instead, it perceives the sudden lack of carbohydrates as a famine. This triggers two protective, but damaging, responses:

Muscle Breakdown (Gluconeogenesis): The body perceives the lack of carbs as a severe threat and aggressively breaks down its own muscle and organ tissue to create sugar. This process keeps cortisol and systemic inflammation chronically high.

Thyroid Down-Regulation: Strict low-carb diets can decrease the liver's ability to convert inactive thyroid hormone (T4) into the active form (T3). The metabolism essentially drops into "low power mode" to hold onto every ounce of stored energy.

For these highly stressed individuals, aggressively pushing for ketosis backfires. They must focus on signaling metabolic safety first.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: The Trap Nobody Warns You About
text:
The section above is about people who are already depleted. But there's a way this goes wrong in perfectly healthy women, and I see it more than anything else.

Low-carb eating suppresses appetite. That's one of its best features — and it's the trap.

When you're genuinely not hungry, you don't eat. Not restricting. Not white-knuckling. Just... not hungry, so lunch gets skipped, and the day ends with two meals that didn't have much in them.

Do that for a few weeks and your body concludes food is scarce. Thyroid output drops. Your cycle changes. Your hands get cold. Hair starts thinning. Progress stalls — and then stalls harder, because the instinct is to cut further.

There's also a sex difference worth knowing. In one study of a single day of fasting, the women's stress hormone rhythm shifted measurably — running higher and peaking earlier. In the men, nothing moved at all.

One study, and it needs replicating. But it points the same way as everything else in this chapter: women appear more sensitive to the stress of restriction, and most low-carb and fasting protocols were built on research in men.

What to Do

For your first month, don't trust your appetite as a guide to how much to eat. Eat your protein on a schedule whether you want it or not.

And if you feel worse rather than better after the first couple of weeks — eat more.

That is almost always the correction, and it is almost always the last thing anyone tries.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Who Should Do This With Medical Supervision
text:
One Important Warning About Diabetes Medication

If you take medication for diabetes, talk to your doctor before you start this. Not because low-carb eating is wrong for you — it may be exactly right. But some medications need adjusting, and one needs real care.

There's a class of diabetes drug you need to know about. The generic names all end in "-flozin" — Jardiance, Farxiga, Invokana, and others. Check your bottle.

These are now also prescribed for heart failure and kidney disease, sometimes in people who don't have diabetes at all. So check regardless.

These drugs work by making your kidneys flush extra sugar out through your urine. That's how they lower blood sugar.

Here's the problem when you combine them with very low carbohydrate.

Ketones are safe at the levels this chapter is about. If they climb much higher, they can turn your blood acidic — a real emergency called ketoacidosis.

Normally there's a warning sign: your blood sugar goes high at the same time, and that's the flag that tells everyone something is wrong.

These medications remove the warning sign. They keep flushing sugar out, so your blood sugar stays normal — or even low — while your ketones keep climbing.

So you can be in real trouble with a blood sugar reading that looks completely fine. Doctors miss it for exactly this reason, and so do patients.

What to do: don't start cutting carbohydrates until you've talked to whoever prescribes it. It's a five-minute conversation. Say: "I'm planning to significantly reduce my carbohydrates. I know that can raise ketoacidosis risk on this medication. How do you want to handle it?"

And know the warning signs regardless — nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, deep or rapid breathing, unusual fatigue or confusion, fruity-smelling breath. If those show up, get seen the same day and tell them you're on this medication and you've changed your diet. Don't wait for your blood sugar to go high, because it may not.

And Four More

Insulin, or the older diabetes pills (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride). These lower your blood sugar regardless of what you eat. Cut carbohydrates without adjusting the dose and it can drop too far. Your prescriber needs to know first.

Blood pressure medication. Eating this way lowers blood pressure — that's good, and it means your dose may become too strong. If you get lightheaded standing up, that's usually not a reason to abandon the diet. It's a reason to get your dose reviewed.

If you're pregnant or trying to conceive, this isn't the time.

If you've had your gallbladder removed or don't tolerate fat well, a very high-fat diet may be genuinely difficult. Don't conclude low-carb isn't for you before addressing digestion — Lesson 11 covers what helps.

And if food is a source of real fear for you, or you have a history of an eating disorder, please talk to someone who knows you before adopting any restrictive framework. This book is written for women whose relationship with food is broadly intact. If that isn't where you are, this isn't the right tool — and that's not a failing.

None of this is a warning against low-carb eating. It's a warning against doing it without telling your doctor you've changed something significant. She can't adjust for what she doesn't know about.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: The Menopause Connection: Why This Matters More After 45
text:
If you're in perimenopause or past it, this may be the most important chapter in the book.

Estradiol is your brain's fuel manager. That isn't a metaphor. Estrogen controls how your brain takes up and uses glucose — it regulates the transporters that bring sugar into your neurons and the machinery that burns it.

As estradiol declines, that system comes apart. Research from the University of Arizona, published in Nature Reviews Endocrinology, describes it directly: during the perimenopausal transition, the estrogen system becomes uncoupled from your brain's energy machinery. The glucose transporters in your neurons decline. And brain hypometabolism — your brain literally producing less energy — appears alongside it.

Brain imaging in postmenopausal women confirms it. There's a measurable decline in how much glucose the brain uses, most pronounced in the same region affected earliest in Alzheimer's disease.

This is why the brain fog is real. It isn't stress, or age, or your imagination. Your brain's primary fuel system is being dismantled, and nobody told you that was part of this.

And Here's What Your Brain Does About It

It doesn't give up. It switches fuels. It starts using ketones.

In the research, the aging female brain increases the transporters that bring ketones in and the enzymes needed to use them. The shift happens automatically — it's the brain's own adaptation to losing access to glucose.

So your brain is already reaching for ketones. The only question is where it gets them.

And this is the part that changes everything. If you're not producing ketones from your diet, your brain will make them from whatever it can find — including breaking down its own white matter. The insulation around your own neurons becomes fuel. Animal research suggests prolonged reliance on that source damages tissue.

Your brain, short of fuel, will consume itself to keep running.

When you eat in a way that produces ketones, you aren't forcing your brain onto an unnatural fuel. You're supplying the fuel it's already asking for, so it doesn't have to take it from your own tissue.

The Rest of What Estradiol Was Doing

Your brain isn't the only system affected. Estradiol was also:

Protecting your muscle. Without it, muscle loss accelerates — which matters enormously, because muscle is where your blood sugar goes. Lesson 17.

Supporting your mitochondria. Lesson 4.

Keeping inflammation down. Lessons 10 and 11.

Influencing where you store fat — the shift toward the middle that most women notice first, without changing anything they eat. Lesson 9.

Ketones touch every one of those. Alternative brain fuel. Mitochondrial support. Reduced inflammatory signalling. And lower insulin, which changes where fat goes.

This is what Dr. Ben Bikman means when he says that as estradiol begins to wane, there's real justification for allowing your ketones to wax.

They aren't a replacement for estrogen. They're support for the systems estrogen used to carry.

Two Honest Notes

This is not an argument against hormone therapy. Hormone therapy addresses the decline directly, it's a legitimate medical option, and the risk picture has been substantially revised since the reporting that frightened a generation of women and their doctors. That's a conversation for you and a practitioner who's current on the research — and it isn't one I'm qualified to have for you. The two approaches address different parts of the same problem.

And this is active research rather than settled fact. The brain's shift toward ketones in menopause is well documented. Whether dietary ketones improve long-term outcomes in women is still being studied — the researchers proposing it call perimenopause a "window of opportunity," which is the language of a promising hypothesis, not a proven treatment. I think the reasoning is strong. You should know it's reasoning.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Do You Have to Do This Forever?
text:
No. And for most people, no is the better answer.

The point of the deep phase is to restore an ability you'd lost — running on fat without falling apart. Once you have it, the goal shifts from being in ketosis to being able to get there easily.

A metabolically flexible body handles a bowl of rice without a crash and slides into fat-burning overnight without drama. That's the destination. Strict ketosis is usually the road, not the address.

How long the strict phase takes varies — a few months is common, longer if insulin resistance has been building for decades. And some people genuinely do best staying low long-term.

What matters is that you're choosing it rather than trapped in it.

If the thought of adding back a sweet potato feels frightening, that's worth paying attention to — and Lesson 18 is about exactly that.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: True Metabolic Flexibility
text: You do not need to be in a state of deep ketosis 100% of the time to be healthy. The ultimate goal is metabolic flexibility. This is the body’s ability to seamlessly transition back and forth. When you eat carbohydrates, your body should be able to burn that glucose efficiently. When you stop eating, your insulin should drop quickly, and your body should effortlessly switch to burning stored fat and producing ketones without experiencing crashes, shakes, or intense cravings. A metabolically flexible body is resilient, energetic, and highly efficient at managing its energy.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: Key Insight
text: Ketones produce significantly fewer free radicals than glucose and act as powerful signaling molecules that protect muscle tissue, enhance cognitive function, and suppress appetite naturally.

doc_title: Lesson 8: Ketones and Metabolic Flexibility
heading: What You Just Learned
text:
- Ketones are produced when insulin is low and serve as a clean, stable, superior fuel source for both the brain and the body.
- The "keto flu" is a temporary energy transition that can be managed effectively with electrolytes and B vitamin supplementation.
- For women in menopause, ketone production provides critical metabolic support that compensates for the decline in estrogen's insulin-sensitizing effects.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Overview
text:
Ancestral whole foods form the foundation of a balanced plate

When you understand that your body operates on hormonal signals rather than just mathematical equations of energy, the way you look at a plate of food fundamentally changes. You are no longer asking, "How much energy does this contain?" You are asking, "What signal is this sending to my body?"

To create an environment where your metabolism thrives, your blood sugar remains stable, and your body can effortlessly burn stored energy, you must structure your meals strategically.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: The Foundation: Protein
text:
Protein should be the undisputed foundation of every meal you eat. It is the most essential macronutrient for human survival and metabolic health. When you consume high-quality protein (like beef, eggs, poultry, and fish), it provides the amino acids necessary to maintain and build muscle tissue. Because muscle is the primary engine of your metabolism, protecting it is your highest priority.

Furthermore, protein is highly satiating. It triggers the release of fullness hormones (like GLP-1 and PYY) while simultaneously requiring a significant amount of internal energy just to digest and process it. This is known as the thermic effect of food.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: How Much Protein? Let's Be Specific
text:
I've told you protein is the foundation of every meal. That's useless without a number.

The number

1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram per day. For most women, toward the upper end.

And here's something that will surprise you: that's the current federal recommendation.

In January 2026, the Dietary Guidelines for Americans were updated — raising protein from the 0.8 grams per kilogram that had stood for eighty-four years to 1.2–1.6. For a 150-pound woman that's roughly 82 to 109 grams a day. Roughly double.

Where the old number came from

The 0.8 figure was never meant to be a target.

The researcher whose work produced it wrote, plainly, what it was: "intended as a minimum value... the lowest level that will maintain nitrogen balance in nearly all healthy individuals."

The floor below which you start visibly breaking down. Not the amount to build muscle, or support a working thyroid, or keep a metabolism running for another fifty years.

And it sat there for eighty-four years. Three generations of women were handed the floor and told it was the goal.

What makes that stranger: in the 1890s the USDA recommended over 110 grams a day. Atwater — the same man whose calorie formula is still on your food labels — set his standard at 125. It took until 2026 to get back to a number we already had in 1900.

Calculate it from your goal weight

This matters and almost nobody gets it right.

If you're carrying extra weight, your protein need is set by the tissue that's metabolically active — the muscle and organs you have and want to keep. Fat tissue barely uses protein. So using your current weight gives you a number that's too high.

Use the weight you're aiming for. If you're already at a healthy weight with decent muscle, use your actual weight. If you lift seriously, go higher.

Per meal, not just per day

Muscle building isn't triggered by protein trickling in across the day. It needs a large enough dose in one sitting to flip the switch.

Spread 60 grams thinly across three meals and you may miss the threshold at all three. Concentrate 90 grams into three real servings and you hit it three times.

And the number goes up with age

This is the most important thing in this section and the least known.

As you get older, your muscles become less responsive to the same amount of protein. A portion that built muscle at 30 may not maintain it at 60.

Your protein requirement rises at exactly the age most women start eating less of it. Appetite drops. Cooking for fewer people. Meat feels heavy. And the requirement goes the other way.

If you take one number from this entire book, take this one.

Can you eat too much?

Yes, but it takes more than you'd think — and I'm raising it because I'm watching a lot of people overshoot.

Above roughly 2 grams per kilogram, more protein stops doing much for anyone who isn't a competitive athlete. Beyond that you're just eating more protein.

Some people eating all-meat diets are at triple the target. Two things happen. Protein crowds out fat, so total energy can quietly fall short. And fasting blood sugar can rise — very high protein with essentially no carbohydrate raises the hormone that tells your liver to release glucose. Readings of 100–110 are common in long-term carnivore eaters.

That's usually adaptive rather than diabetic — your muscles are deliberately sparing glucose for your brain. But read it alongside fasting insulin and HbA1c, never alone. Lesson 3.

So what does "moderate protein" mean? You'll hear keto described that way, and most people hear it as not much. It means 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram of your goal weight — considerably more than you're eating now, and nowhere near 300 grams.

One note: if you have reduced kidney function, protein intake is a genuine medical question. Higher protein hasn't been shown to harm healthy kidneys — but don't raise it substantially without talking to your doctor.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Protein Was Never About Muscle
text:
Now here's why protein matters far more than muscle.

When you eat protein, your body takes it apart into amino acids — about twenty building blocks. Nine of them your body cannot make. They have to come from food, every day, or you start taking them out of yourself.

Your thyroid hormone is made from protein

Thyroid hormone — the thing that sets your metabolic rate, the subject of an entire chapter of this book — is built from an amino acid called tyrosine, with iodine attached.

Not supported by protein. Made of it.

So is the molecule that carries fat into your cells

Remember the doorway from Lesson 8 — the one fat has to be carried through to be burned?

The carrier is called carnitine, and your body builds it from two amino acids — using vitamin C to assemble it.

No carnitine, no fat through the door. Your ability to burn fat depends on a molecule made from protein.

And your master antioxidant

Your cells' most important protective compound, glutathione, is built from three amino acids.

This one matters more than it sounds. In Lesson 5 you learned that inflammation blocks your body from activating thyroid hormone. The way it does that is by depleting glutathione. So the raw materials for glutathione are also raw materials for a working thyroid.

The short version

Amino acids also build your neurotransmitters — tryptophan becomes serotonin, tyrosine becomes dopamine. They build every enzyme in your body, your immune cells, your collagen, and the protein part of every hormone you have.

Protein isn't the muscle macronutrient. It's the raw material for the machinery.

Which is why eating too little doesn't just cost you muscle. It quietly limits your thyroid, your fat burning, your antioxidant defenses, and your ability to repair anything.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Not All Protein Contains the Same Things
text:
Different foods contain different amino acids, in different amounts. Twenty grams of protein from two sources is not the same twenty grams.

Animal proteins — meat, fish, eggs, dairy — contain all nine essential amino acids in roughly the proportions your body needs. That's why they're called complete.

Plant proteins are usually short on at least one. Grains tend to be low in lysine; beans tend to be low in methionine. Not a problem if you eat a variety — that's the reasoning behind rice and beans, and behind every traditional cuisine that pairs a grain with a legume. But it means you need more total plant protein to get the same usable amount.

And one amino acid does the triggering

Of the nine, one is the signal that tells your muscle to start building: leucine.

This is why the per meal amount matters. You need enough leucine in one sitting to flip the switch — and leucine is concentrated in animal protein, whey, and eggs.

Another reason 30 grams at each of three meals beats 90 at dinner.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: The One Almost Everyone Is Short On
text:
This is the part I most want you to know, because the fix is simple.

Glycine.

It's technically non-essential — your body can make it. The problem is that it can't make enough.

In 2009, biochemists did the arithmetic on how much glycine the human body requires versus how much it can produce. They found a shortfall of roughly 10 grams a day — and showed it's structural. Not about eating badly or having a slow metabolism. The pathway itself has a ceiling, and our needs exceed it.

They called it "a weak link in metabolism" and argued glycine should be reclassified as essential.

Why you need so much

Glycine is the main ingredient in collagen — it occupies every third position in the collagen molecule. And collagen is the most abundant protein in your body: roughly eight pounds of it, in your bones, cartilage, tendons, skin, and the framework holding every organ together.

It's also required for glutathione (your master antioxidant — glycine appears to be the rate-limiting ingredient), creatine, heme (the iron-carrying part of your blood and the iron built into your energy chain from Lesson 4), your liver's detoxification pathways, and sleep and temperature regulation.

And why modern diets run short

We stopped eating the parts of the animal that contain it.

Glycine is concentrated in skin, connective tissue, cartilage, tendon, and bone — the gelatinous parts. Muscle meat, which is nearly all we eat now, is comparatively low in it.

Your great-grandmother made stock from bones. She ate the skin, the tougher cuts, the parts that turn gelatinous when they cook. We eat chicken breast.

So we get plenty of the amino acids concentrated in muscle and very little of the one concentrated in everything else.

There's also a balance problem

Muscle meat is high in methionine, another essential amino acid. You need it.

But in animal research, a high-methionine, low-glycine pattern accelerates aging, while glycine appears to counterbalance it.

Modern eating produces exactly the wrong ratio: plenty of methionine from muscle meat and eggs, very little glycine because we skip the rest.

The answer isn't less meat. It's the rest of the animal.

What to do

One of the easiest fixes in this book:

Bone broth or stock. Real stock that gels when it cools — that gelling is the collagen.

Eat the gelatinous cuts. Oxtail, shanks, short ribs, chuck, chicken thighs with the skin, anything slow-cooked with the bone in. These cost less than the lean cuts — a rare case where the better choice is cheaper.

Eat the skin. On chicken, on fish.

Collagen or gelatin powder if the cooking isn't realistic. It isn't a magic supplement — it's the part of the animal you stopped eating, in a jar.

A note on the research: the 10-gram shortfall is calculated rather than measured directly, and supplementation trials in healthy people are limited. But the calculation is sound, the biochemistry behind the ceiling is well understood, and the fix is food your ancestors ate routinely.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Putting Protein Together
text:
Eat enough — the amount from earlier in this chapter.

Mostly from animal sources, because they contain all nine essentials in usable proportions and the most leucine.

Spread across meals, so you hit the trigger more than once a day.

And eat more of the animal than the muscle. Bones, skin, connective tissue, the slow-cooked cuts. Whole animal, not just the lean parts — same principle as whole food. The parts we discarded turned out to matter.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: The Fuel: Healthy Fats and the Fat Cell Dilemma
text:
For decades, we were falsely taught that eating fat makes you fat. Biologically, this makes no sense. Fat is the only macronutrient that has essentially zero impact on insulin. When you eat fat, your body receives a signal of abundant fuel without the storage-triggering spike of insulin.

However, the type of fat you eat dictates how your fat cells behave. To understand this, you must understand why some heavy people are metabolically healthy, while some thin people develop type 2 diabetes. It all comes down to how your body stores energy:

Hyperplasia (Healthy Storage)

When energy is abundant, some bodies naturally multiply their fat cells, creating brand new, small, healthy fat cells to store the energy. This keeps the person highly insulin sensitive, even if they carry a lot of extra weight.

Hypertrophy (Sick Storage)

Other people have a genetic limit on the number of fat cells they can make. Instead of multiplying, their existing fat cells simply inflate like balloons. When a single fat cell gets too big (hypertrophied), it becomes sick, heavily inflamed, and highly insulin resistant. It begins leaking fatty acids into the bloodstream. This is why a physically thin person can suddenly develop severe metabolic disease—their limited fat cells reached maximum capacity and became sick.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: The Hormone That Goes the Other Way
text:
There's a second thing that happens when fat cells inflate, and it's easy to miss.

Healthy fat tissue produces a hormone called adiponectin — one of the genuinely helpful ones. It improves insulin sensitivity, lowers inflammation, and encourages your cells to burn fat rather than store it.

Hypertrophied fat cells make less of it. As they inflate, they produce less adiponectin and more inflammatory signals — and more leptin, the one your brain has already stopped hearing.

So sick fat storage isn't passive. The unhelpful signal goes up and the helpful one goes down, at the same time.

Deep abdominal fat produces even less adiponectin than fat under the skin — which is part of why your waist measurement tells you more than the scale. Worth remembering when the number won't move: a tape measure can see progress a scale can't, because the scale can't tell the difference between losing fat and losing muscle.

Advanced metabolic research highlights a massive problem in the modern diet: the overconsumption of industrial seed oils (like soybean, canola, corn, and sunflower oils). These oils are highly unstable and packed with linoleic acid. When consumed in excess, linoleic acid forces your body into hypertrophy. Instead of allowing your fat cells to multiply safely, seed oils force your existing fat cells to rapidly inflate, become inflamed, and drive systemic insulin resistance.

To support your metabolism, completely remove industrial seed oils from your diet. Replace them with ancestral, stable fats: butter, ghee, tallow, coconut oil, olive oil, and the natural fats found in whole cuts of meat and eggs. These fats support hormone production, keep your brain healthy, and provide deep, long-lasting energy.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: How Exactly Does This Happen?
text:
Two ways, and the second is the one operating in you right now.

Linoleic acid converts in your body to arachidonic acid, which directly drives fat tissue development through a specific signalling pathway. Researchers demonstrated it cleanly: mice whose mothers ate a linoleic-acid-rich diet were 40% heavier shortly after weaning — and the effect disappeared completely in mice bred without the receptor that pathway uses.

Same calories. Different fat. Different bodies.

The second route is the one that matters for you now. Omega-6 excess drives inflammation, and inflammation blocks the healthy kind of fat storage.

When researchers examined insulin-resistant people, their fat tissue had lost much of its ability to make new fat cells — with the specific genetic switches for that process turned down. The culprit was an inflammatory signal produced by their own fat tissue.

So the sequence is: seed oils feed inflammation. Inflammation shuts down your ability to make new small fat cells. And the energy has nowhere to go except into the cells you already have. They inflate, become inflamed themselves, and the cycle tightens.

Remember this in Lesson 10. The same inflammation doing this is what instructs your body to build insulin-blocking ceramides. One problem wearing two costumes.

And the Encouraging Half

Omega-3 fats appear to do the reverse. Studies show fish oil reducing fat cell size while increasing the formation of new small ones.

This axis moves in both directions depending on what you eat.

It's Not the Fat. It's What They Do to It.

Let me be precise about what I'm asking you to avoid.

Your body needs omega-6. You'd get sick without it. A handful of walnuts, some sunflower seeds, an avocado — that's omega-6 in the form nature made it: wrapped inside the food, protected from air and light by the vitamin E that came with it.

What happens in an industrial refinery is a different thing entirely.

The oil gets extracted. It's heated past 400 degrees to strip out the smell — which also strips out the vitamin E protecting it. Then it sits on a shelf under fluorescent lights for months. Then it goes into a restaurant fryer and is heated over and over for days.

Fragile fat, stripped of its protection, heated repeatedly. What comes out is not what went in. It's full of broken-down fragments your body has to deal with — and those fragments drive exactly the inflammation we've been discussing.

So the rule isn't "avoid omega-6." It's this:

Eat fat in the form it came in. Avoid fat that's been refined, bottled, and reheated.

Olive oil, butter, avocado, coconut, tallow, whole nuts and seeds — fine.

Canola, soybean, corn, cottonseed, safflower, sunflower in a clear plastic bottle — and especially anything fried in a restaurant — not fine.

By applying the Fiber First rule — eating your fibrous vegetables and high-quality protein before your carbohydrates — you completely change the biological response to that exact same meal.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: The Lever: Carbohydrates and "Metabolic Safety"
text:
If protein is the foundation and fat is the primary fuel, carbohydrates should be viewed as a lever that you pull based on your activity level and metabolic health. For a healthy individual looking to burn fat, pulling the carbohydrate lever low is highly effective.

However, for individuals with stressed adrenals, chronic illness, or those who feel constantly "wired but tired," dropping carbohydrates too low sends a massive famine signal to the brain, spiking adrenaline and cortisol. In these cases, we must use the Carbohydrate Safety Principle.

Instead of strict elimination, the goal is to incorporate "safe starches"—like sweet potatoes, plantains, winter squash, and whole fruits. These easy-to-digest carbohydrates provide a steady supply of glucose, which actively inhibits the breakdown of muscle tissue, lowers stress hormones like adrenaline, and supports healthy thyroid function.

Carb Back-Loading for Sleep and Stress

If you struggle with high stress and poor sleep, strategic carbohydrate timing is vital. Cortisol should naturally be highest in the morning and lowest at night. Eating a high-protein, low-carb breakfast supports this natural morning energy. However, incorporating a moderate portion of safe starches with your dinner helps actively lower evening cortisol and supports the production of serotonin and melatonin, easing the nervous system into deep, restorative sleep.

This isn't just theory. In a controlled study, people who ate a carbohydrate meal four hours before bed fell asleep measurably faster than those eating a lower-glycemic version. A later review found carbohydrate quantity and quality significantly affected how fast people fell asleep, how efficiently they slept, and how much deep and REM sleep they got.

Two details make the difference:

Timing. Four hours before bed worked. One hour before bed did not. So this means dinner — a real dinner, finished with time to spare. Not a bedtime snack.

Quality. Use your safe starches: sweet potato, winter squash, plantain. Not dessert. High-sugar food late at night suppresses melatonin and fragments sleep, which is the opposite of what you're after.

You'll sometimes see this explained as carbohydrate boosting serotonin. That mechanism barely works once there's protein in the meal — and your dinner will have protein. The effect is real; that explanation isn't the reason.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: What About Artificial Sweeteners?
text:
It is theorized that some sweeteners may trigger an insulin response in some people, just from the taste. The research isn't settled — it seems to depend on the sweetener, the form, and the individual. Worth keeping in mind, because someone who responds strongly would be quietly keeping her fat-burning gates shut with something she believed was free.

But there's a second effect that's better documented and may matter more.

A 2025 study scanned the brains of 75 people after they drank sucralose, real sugar, or water. Sucralose increased activity in the hunger center of the brain and increased their actual hunger by about 17%. And it produced no fullness hormones at all. As the lead researcher put it: there's a sweetness signal, but no hormone signal telling you you're full.

Effects were strongest in people already carrying extra weight. And women showed bigger changes in that brain region than men.

So the real problem isn't insulin. It's that you get the promise without the payoff, and your body responds by asking for more.

Which points at the actual answer, and it isn't a product. The goal isn't finding a sweet thing that's safe. It's no longer needing the sweet thing. Sweet cravings are largely learned and maintained by exposure — and they fade faster than most people expect. Try two weeks without and watch.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Alcohol: The One Nobody Wants to Talk About
text:
This deserves its own section, because for a lot of women it's the single biggest obstacle and they have no idea why.

Your body treats alcohol as something to get rid of, not something to use. It goes to the front of the queue — and while your liver is clearing it, fat burning essentially stops. Not slows. Pauses.

So the problem isn't mainly the calories in the drink. It's that two glasses of wine can shut down fat burning for hours — during a window when everything else you did that day had you well positioned.

Three more things stack on top:

It fragments your sleep even when it helps you fall asleep — which feeds into the hunger hormones from Lesson 7 and the stress hormones in Lesson 13.

It reliably lowers restraint around food, usually at night, when the pull is already strongest.

And the liver clearing it is the same liver doing everything in Lesson 11 — including converting your thyroid hormone into its active form.

You don't have to quit. But if your progress has stalled and there's a nightly drink in the picture, that's the first thing I'd test — and the test is two weeks without, not one. One week is mostly water weight.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: The "Fiber First" Rule: Food Sequencing
text:
It is not just what you eat that determines your metabolic response; the order in which you eat your food plays a massive role in how your body handles blood sugar. This is known as food sequencing.

If you eat carbohydrates on an empty stomach, they are rapidly broken down and absorbed into the bloodstream, causing a sharp spike in glucose and a massive surge of insulin. However, if you apply the "Fiber First" rule—eating your fibrous vegetables and high-quality protein before you eat your carbohydrates—you completely change the biological response.

The fiber and protein create a physical matrix in your digestive tract, naturally slowing down gastric emptying. When the carbohydrates finally arrive, their absorption is drastically delayed. This simple shift in sequencing can significantly blunt your blood sugar and insulin spike, keeping your body in a stable, fat-burning state for much longer after a meal—without changing a single ingredient on your plate.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Why Pizza Is Different
text:
There's a reason certain combinations feel impossible to stop eating, and it isn't a character weakness.

When both fuels arrive at once, in quantity, your cells congest. Not because they can't use either one — because they can't commit to one while the other keeps arriving. The result is half-finished byproducts and cellular exhaust, and that exhaust interferes with insulin's signal directly. Lesson 4 covers what's happening inside the cell.

And nature almost never packages the two together. Nothing that grows is both high in fat and high in refined starch at high density. Bread and butter. Cheese and crackers. Pastries. Chips. Ice cream. That combination has to be manufactured.

There's a second reason those foods are hard to stop eating, and it has nothing to do with your cells. When researchers put people in a scanner, foods combining fat and refined carbohydrate were valued more than the sum of their parts — people worked harder and paid more for them, and it wasn't explained by calories or even by how much they said they liked the food.

So it's engineered on two levels. The combination overwhelms your cells, and it also overrides the signal that tells you to stop.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Why Your Body Might Burn Fuel Differently Than Your Friend's
text:
The Randle Cycle explains more than just what happens inside a single meal. It also explains why the exact same diet can produce wildly different results in two different people. When you eat fat, your body has a choice: burn that fat you just ate for immediate energy, or reach into your own stored body fat instead. Research shows your body actually prioritizes the fat sitting in your bloodstream from your last meal before it will touch what's stored on your hips, waist, or thighs.

This is why some people can eat generously on a ketogenic diet—plenty of fat, plenty of food—and still lose weight steadily. Their bodies are efficient at reaching past the dietary fat and pulling from stored reserves. Other people can eat the exact same way, stay in ketosis, avoid gaining weight, and still find their stored fat barely budges. Their bodies are simply better at burning what's freshly eaten than what's already stored.1

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Your Fat Cells Are Not a Storage Unit
text:
You probably picture fat storage like a warehouse. Energy comes in, gets locked away, stays there until you burn it off. That isn't how it works at all.

Your fat cells are breaking down and rebuilding fat constantly — right now, and while you sleep.

How stored fat is built

Stored fat is called a triglyceride, and the name describes it: three fatty acids on one glycerol backbone. Think of the glycerol as a rack holding three items.

To store fat, your body needs both the fatty acids and the rack.

And here's the surprising part: when a fat cell breaks a triglyceride apart, it cannot reuse its own rack. Fat cells lack the enzyme needed to recycle glycerol. The rack gets released into your bloodstream and floats away.

So every time a fat cell stores fat again, it has to build a brand new rack from scratch.

Where the rack comes from

When you eat carbohydrate, your fat cells build racks easily — glucose is the raw material and it's right there. Carbohydrate makes storage easy.

When you don't, your fat cells build racks anyway — from lactate, from amino acids, from other available materials. The pathway was discovered in 1967.

And here's what should catch your attention: your body turns that pathway UP during fasting. The gene for the key enzyme is actively switched on when food is scarce.

Your body has a dedicated system for rebuilding fat, and it runs hardest when you're not eating.

Which explains the most frustrating thing about fat loss

In fasting humans, researchers have measured as much as 60% of the fatty acids released from fat cells being put straight back into storage.

Released. Not burned. Repackaged.

Scientists call this a futile cycle, and it literally is — it costs your body six units of energy currency to reattach three fatty acids. Your body spends energy to store fat it just released.

This is what's actually happening when people say they're in fat-burning mode and not losing fat.

You are releasing fat. Most of it is going back in. Whether your fat stores shrink depends on whether, across days and weeks, more comes out than goes back — not on whether the door is open.

So what determines the direction?

Two things, and they're both familiar.

How much fat is released — mostly insulin. Lower insulin, more release. Lessons 2 and 8.

How much gets burned versus repackaged — whether your tissues actually need the energy. If you've eaten enough fat to meet your needs, your body has no reason to burn what it just released. So it pays the cost and puts it back.

Which is the honest answer to a question that confuses a lot of people. If low-carb means low insulin, and low insulin means fat release, why am I not losing fat?

Because release isn't loss. You've opened the door, and your body is walking the fat right back through it — because you gave it enough dietary fat that it doesn't need yours.

So once you're fat-adapted, the lever is usually the added fats. The butter in the coffee, the extra oil, the fat bombs. Useful during the transition. Frequently the reason nothing moves afterward.

And one genuinely beautiful thing

Remember the rack has to leave the fat cell because it can't be reused there?

It goes to your liver — and your liver turns it into glucose.

So there's a complete loop running in your body right now:

Stored fat breaks apart → fatty acids and glycerolFatty acids → burned for energy, or converted to ketones for your brainGlycerol → to the liver → becomes the small amount of glucose your body still needs

That's how you maintain normal blood sugar on almost no dietary carbohydrate. Part of it is being made from the backbone of your own fat.

One correction worth making

You may have heard that you can't store fat without carbohydrate. Partly right mechanically, wrong as an absolute.

Carbohydrate makes building the rack much easier, so storage is easier when it's around. But your body can build the rack without it, and it will.

I'm telling you because I'd rather you hear it from me. There are no loopholes in your metabolism — only conditions that make one direction easier than the other. Lowering insulin makes release easier. That's real and valuable. It isn't a door that locks behind you.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Fat Isn't All Stored in One Place
text:
When we say "body fat," most people picture one thing. Your body keeps it in four places, and they behave completely differently.

In your fat cells — what you see in the mirror.

Inside your muscle cells — small droplets stored right next to the machinery that burns them. This one is a fuel tank, not a storage unit.

In your liver — where it causes problems if it piles up. Lesson 11.

In your blood — travelling to where it's needed. This is what a blood test measures.

Four separate compartments. More in one doesn't mean more in another. And one of them is actually a sign of fitness.

The Finding That Surprised Everyone

Fat inside muscle was assumed to be bad. In sedentary people it tracks reliably with insulin resistance.

Then researchers measured endurance athletes.

Athletes have as much fat inside their muscles as people with type 2 diabetes. And they're among the most insulin-sensitive people you can find.

Same fat. Same place. Opposite health. Scientists called it the athlete's paradox, and it took ten years to solve.

And the Answer Changes How You Should Think About This

Stored fat inside a muscle cell is harmless. It's a fuel tank.

The damage happens when fatty acids get turned into other compounds instead — and trained muscle has far fewer of those. Lesson 10.

Then researchers found something that flips the intuition. The faster someone was packaging fat into storage inside her muscle, the healthier her blood sugar was.

Storing fat safely is how your muscle protects itself. A fatty acid parked as storage can't be turned into something harmful.

So the Goal Was Never "Less Fat"

Stored fat isn't your enemy. It's your energy system. What you want isn't less of it — it's fat that moves. In and out, stored where it belongs, used when needed.

A trained woman has more fat inside her muscles than an untrained one and is metabolically healthier. Because hers is cycling through instead of sitting there.

It isn't how much you store. It's whether it moves.

One thing so this doesn't confuse you: your blood triglycerides are a different pool, and lower really is better there. Exercise lowers those, because trained muscle gets much better at pulling fat out of your bloodstream and using it. Two pools, opposite directions, both good.

Efficient Stored-Fat Burners

Some bodies are highly efficient at reaching past recently eaten fat to tap into stored reserves. These individuals often see steady fat loss on a well-formulated low-carb or ketogenic diet, even with generous fat intake.

Dietary-Fat Preferential Burners

Other bodies preferentially burn whatever fat was just eaten before ever reaching stored fat. These individuals may stay weight-stable on a high-fat diet without much fat loss, even without gaining weight.

This isn't a character flaw or a sign you're doing something wrong. Genuine genetic differences exist in the enzymes and transporters responsible for fat-burning capacity,2 and a history of past weight loss and regain can also reduce how efficiently your body burns fat, even at the very same body weight as someone who has never struggled with their weight. This is one of the many reasons a truly personalized approach matters more than a one-size-fits-all rule.

Fat burning and fat loss are not automatically the same thing. Your body can be actively burning fat all day and still not be touching your stored reserves, if it keeps reaching for what you just ate instead.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate
heading: Exercise and the Randle Cycle
text:
Exercise adds another layer to this same competition. When you exercise, especially with resistance training or higher-intensity movement, you deplete the glycogen (stored carbohydrate) in your muscles. This temporarily makes your muscles unusually receptive to absorbing carbohydrates without the same insulin spike they'd normally trigger. In practical terms, the day you exercise hard is often the day your body is best equipped to handle the carbohydrates in your meal.3

Beyond meal composition and exercise timing, several other factors can prevent your body from reaching a fat-burning state, even on a well-formulated low-carb plan. We cover these in depth in Lesson 13, including chronic stress and elevated cortisol, poor sleep, a history of chronic dieting, systemic inflammation, and certain medications.

doc_title: Lesson 9: Balancing Your Plate

text: Industrial seed oils force your fat cells into hypertrophy — sick, inflamed, oversized storage — rather than allowing them to multiply safely, directly driving systemic insulin resistance.
